Workers say AI timed their toilet breaks. Their employer says it isn't even AI

More than 300 distribution workers at The Warehouse, New Zealand's largest retailer, walked off the job in Auckland and Christchurch on Thursday.

Their union says AI tracks their bathroom breaks, and that some staff ended up urinating and defecating in the aisles. "Having supervisors and managers follow people to the toilet and telling them off for a fundamental right is absolutely ludicrous," organiser Hayley Courtney told RNZ.

The company denies all of it. Its scanning devices measure efficiency, it says, are "not AI as claimed" and have "nothing to do with bathroom use." Of the aisle claims, its people chief said: "This has never happened."

The bigger fear is jobs. Drones now count the stock, and a large robot is coming to pack orders. "Do I look like a robot? No. I don't," said a woman who has worked there for 23 years. The company says the machines haven't cost anyone a permanent job.

⚠️ AI just became Wall Street's biggest fear in a Fed survey, beating inflation and debt

87% of the 23 market insiders the New York Fed polled named AI as a risk to the financial system. In the spring, it was 50%.

They worry about AI stocks falling if profits disappoint, about how the AI build-out is financed, and about cyber risk, from state hackers or from "damage caused by frontier AI models themselves."

The Fed's report says stock prices are high partly because of "market enthusiasm for super intelligence." Debt raised for AI computing passed $680 billion by October, about five times all of 2023.

The largest US banks have close to $1 trillion of exposure to tech giants, data center builders, utilities and the vehicles that fund them.

❗️Nvidia’s AI boom may be built on a risky financial loop.

According to the Wall Street Journal, Nvidia has been financing and guaranteeing loans for AI companies and data center operators that buy its GPUs. The strategy turns them into long-term customers, but also leaves Nvidia exposed if they cannot repay their debts.

The scale is growing rapidly, Nvidia disclosed $530 billion in commitments and guarantees, up from $184 billion just one quarter earlier.

The controversial part is that Nvidia can effectively act as the investor, lender, chip supplier and backup customer for the same companies. It finances data centers, sells them GPUs and sometimes agrees to purchase their unused computing capacity.

CoreWeave and OpenAI are prominent examples. Nvidia owns a stake in CoreWeave and has agreed to buy up to $6.3 billion in unused computing capacity. For OpenAI’s Ohio data center, Nvidia’s guarantee was reportedly reduced from $250 billion to $105 billion.

CFO Colette Kress had reportedly questioned the risks of these arrangements and pushed to reduce some commitments. Now, with Jensen Huang reportedly out of the picture, she is in charge of Nvidia.

The central risk is straightforward. If AI companies struggle to find customers or repay their debts, they may stop buying Nvidia chips. That could turn Nvidia’s financing strategy into a source of pressure on its own revenue.

💻 Tell Claude's new model "never" and it won't budge. Anthropic says what to write instead

Claude Fable 5.2 treats any instruction with "never" as absolute. Its prompting guide suggests "ask for approval before deleting files" over "never delete files" when you still want a say.

Newsletter writer Ruben Hassid turned the guide into lines anyone can paste:

1. Find "always" and "never" in your Claude instructions and memory. In grey areas, write "ask me first".
2. Don't just say "Go". Say what you approve: "Yes, rewrite the 3 welcome emails. Leave the invoice template alone."
3. Tell it to finish:
Finish the whole job before you stop. Don't offer to continue: continue. Ask me before you delete anything.
4. Ask for a report you can read:
End with a recap for someone who saw none of the work: key points first, plain words.

In Anthropic's replay of real coding sessions, its longer finish-the-job text roughly halved the runs that stopped with work left.

🧐 Everyone has the same AI models. A founder's 49-step list starts with what only you have

Greg Isenberg, whose firm Late Checkout builds startups, posted his plan for an "AI pilled" company. Before any agent or tool, it builds the files your agents read:

• A second brain: one folder of notes on how you think, write and decide (Obsidian).
• Voice notes all day (Wispr), with an agent filing every fact, story and decision.
• Every call and meeting recorded (Granola), straight into the brain.
• A facts file: true things agents are allowed to say about you. He says it kills made-up claims.
• A voice file: your 50 best posts, 20 you hate and the words you never use.
• One instruction file on top (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) that agents read before any task.

The other steps cover skills, agent teams, costs and growth, down to "track cost per job. if a job costs more than it earns, fix it or kill it".

His last line:
The models are the same for everyone but your context is the only part that's yours.

🗣 China's leaders understand AI risk "much better than the US government," Geoffrey Hinton says

The Nobel-winning "godfather of AI" said on PBS's Firing Line, aired November 13, that last summer he went to Shanghai and talked to a Politburo member, a protégé of Xi Jinping.

"I believe the Politburo understands this stuff much better than the US government. They are very concerned about these risks and they will collaborate with the US on trying to prevent superintelligence taking over."

That won't happen yet, he said, "while we still have a, how can I say this, maybe a corrupt senile felon in the White House."

Not for two years, he thinks. After that, he expects a "sensible US government" to work with China on superintelligence, much as the US and the Soviet Union did on the dangers of H-bombs in the 1950s.

🗣 Would she fire Sam Altman again? "Oh, for sure," says the OpenAI board member who did

Helen Toner was one of four OpenAI board members who voted to fire Altman in 2023. He came back as CEO, and she left the board.

Asked on The Verge's Decoder podcast whether she would do it the same way again, Toner said: "Oh, for sure. I mean, we went into it knowing that it was going to suck."

Is Altman trustworthy? "I think my stance on that is pretty clear," she said. Then the bigger point: "if our hopes for the future are pinned on any one individual being trustworthy, then we're pretty screwed."

Toner now runs Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology. The people building these systems say the safety problems must be solved within 12 to 24 months. "I think that's terrifying and I hope they're wrong."
